description: Gente que le cope el challange Planet X and SPHEREx
summary:
SkyBlink lets anyone watch the infrared sky change, and find what moves in it. Type a name or coordinates, or spin a 3D celestial sphere and click anywhere, and it builds a short movie of that patch of sky from NASA's SPHEREx mission, so objects that move or vary stand out. Because SPHEREx observes every point at 102 wavelengths, one click on a source gives its spectrum, its light curve and a plain-language object card.

Comparison modes (blink, difference, red/cyan, a visible/infrared curtain) and a time-travel mode that steps from 1950s photographic plates through 2MASS and WISE to SPHEREx make motion visible even for slow objects. A measuring tool turns clicks into a proper motion: we recover Barnard's Star at 10.31 ± 0.44 arcsec/yr (catalog: 10.45) and the brown dwarf WISE 0855 at 8.0 ± 1.5 (catalog: 8.15). The variable star R Draconis shows a 61–66% brightness change across three survey passes.

A guided tour teaches newcomers to find a brown dwarf in a couple of minutes. Every view is shareable by URL, and the tool queries the live archive, so new data releases appear without code changes.
details:
THE IDEA

SPHEREx is photographing more than a billion objects in 102 colors of infrared light. Somewhere in there are comets, brown dwarfs and nearby stars nobody has noticed yet, and the way to find them is simple: look at the same patch of sky at two different times and see what moved. No one person can look at all of it. SkyBlink is built so that anyone can.

WHAT IT FEELS LIKE

You open the site and see the sky as a sphere you can spin, with constellations to get your bearings. Click anywhere, or type a name, and that patch of sky starts blinking between the dates SPHEREx observed it. Things that moved jump. Things that changed brightness flicker. You need no coordinates, no software and no training.

Click on any star and SkyBlink tells you what it is: how far away, how fast it moves, and its spectrum, the fingerprint that shows what it is made of. You can even listen to that spectrum. A time-travel mode steps back through older surveys to photographic plates from the 1950s, so you can watch a nearby star cross the sky over seventy years. On a phone, a "sky window" mode shows the infrared sky in the direction you point the device.

A guided tour takes a first-time visitor through finding a real brown dwarf, one that is invisible in most of SPHEREx's colors and appears only in the reddest ones, in a couple of minutes. After that, they know how to search on their own.

WHY IT MATTERS

Most of the known brown dwarfs were found by volunteers comparing images by eye. SPHEREx adds something earlier surveys did not have, a spectrum for every point of the sky, but only if people can reach it. SkyBlink turns that data into something a curious person can explore in a browser, share with a link, and use to make a real measurement. Every view is a URL, so a teacher can send a class to the same star, and anyone can show others what they found. The interface is in English and Spanish.

IT MEASURES REAL THINGS

This is not only a viewer. With three clicks, the Measure tool recovers the motion of Barnard's Star at 10.31 ± 0.44 arcseconds per year (catalog value: 10.45) and of the brown dwarf WISE 0855 at 8.0 ± 1.5 (catalog: 8.15). The variable star R Draconis shows a 61–66% change in brightness, about ten times the measurement error, while a steady star used as a control stays flat within 3%. All five targets named in the challenge work.

HOW IT IS BUILT

The backend (Python, FastAPI, Astropy) finds the hundreds of SPHEREx exposures covering a field, cleans and aligns them, and stacks them by date and by detector. The browser (TypeScript, React, WebGL, three.js) does all the comparisons on the user's device, so switching views is instant. New fields are built on demand; when NASA's archive is busy, the same images are read from the public cloud copy of the data. Twenty-two showcase fields are ready to open immediately.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We designed for someone who has never done this, then checked that the result still satisfies someone who has. We were careful not to overstate the data: the pixels are large, there are only three or four survey passes so far, bright stars saturate, and close neighbors blend. The tool says so on screen wherever it applies, instead of showing a result that looks better than it is.

Source code: https://github.com/RenzoGiacometti/spherex-explorer
